newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: IMF mission reviews funding to Zambia for 1997.
newsitem.headline: IMF mission reviews funding to Zambia for 1997.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) said on Tuesday it was currently reviewing Zambia's economic performance and discussing funding under the Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF).

"An IMF mission arrived in the country on May 3 for annual consultations with Zambia on all aspects of the economy and to initiate the second-year ESAF arrangement," the IMF's representative in Zambia, Elwaleed Taha, told Reuters.
"The mission will be in the country up to May 13," Taha said, adding that the IMF was likely to release funds for a second year under the ESAF.
The IMF in February endorsed Zambia's economic performance under the first year of ESAF and released SDR 10 million (about $14 million) to the country.
The IMF endorsement means that Paris Club members will reschedule 67 percent of Zambia's debts to them.
Zambia, whose total external debt stands at around $6.38 billion, has a debt-to-exports ratio of 20 percent.

According to Taha, key achievements leading to the IMF endorsement included the reduction of inflation to the lowest annual level in eight years at 35 percent, and a 6.5 percent economic growth in 1996.
Other achievements included an increase in social sector spending at 34.5 percent and progress in the privatisation of state enterprises.
Zambia regained IMF support in December 1995 after clearing arrears to the world body of SDR 830.2 million.
The country was declared ineligible to use IMF financial resources in September 1987 following the accumulation of overdue financial obligations to the IMF.
The Frederick Chiluba government is, meanwhile, struggling to restore normal relations with Western governments following a stand-off over governance concerns last year.

Western governments led by the United States cut or froze aid to this dirt-poor southern African country after the government introduced new laws to ban some candidates from contesting general elections held last November.
The government hosted a donors meeting in London last month at which it tried to persuade Western governments to restore normal aid flows to Zambia.
Donors agreed after the meeting to hold a Consultative Group meeting in early July when they will be expected to make aid pledges for 1997.
A third of the country's $1.1 billion budget for 1997 is dependant on donor aid.
